newsitem.title: UK: British government to fight on after majority goes.
newsitem.headline: British government to fight on after majority goes.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative party suffered a crushing by-election defeat to lose its overall parliamentary majority but insisted on Friday it would carry on in office as long as it could win votes in the House of Commons.
"As long as we have majorities (in parliament) that are deliverable on a regular basis, then we will continue to govern," Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney said.

The opposition Labour Party win in the by-election in the northern England seat of Barnsley East means the 323 Conservative members of parliament are now matched by the same number of opposition legislators.

Labour local council leader Jeff Ennis won 14,683 votes against 1,299 for Conservative Jane Ellison, who finished third to Liberal Democrat candidate David Willis with 1,502. Turnout was just over 33 percent of the electorate of about 53,000.

Ennis was defending a Labour majority of 24,777 votes won by his predecessor Terry Patchett, whose recent death led to the by-election. The fall in the Labour majority was due largely to low turnout in the by-election.
"The government is going to find it increasingly a problem getting its business (through parliament)," Donald Dewar, parliamentary business manager for Labour said.
"The government is now time-expired. The clock is ticking down for them," he told the BBC.

The government, 21 points behind Labour in the last national opinion poll, is desperate to remain in office until May, the last possible month for a general election. It hopes better economic conditions will turn into improved poll ratings. Its position was weakened last week when one of its legislators, Sir John Gorst, said he could no longer promise Prime Minister John Major his automatic support because of a row over hospital facilities in his North London constituency.
But Mawhinney's statement reflected Conservative optimism that it will prove difficult for Labour to unite all the opposition parties against the government in key Commons votes.
In particular, they hope the nine MPs who represent the Ulster Unionist party which seeks to preserve British rule over Northern Ireland will hesitate to turn them out of office.

Barnsley East was one of the last tests of public opinion before the next general election. But another by-election is pending in the north-western seat of Wirral South following the death of Conservative Barry Porter.

If the Conservatives were to lose this seat, which Porter won with an 8,183 vote majority at the 1992 general election, it would also lose its majority in key parliamentary committees, making governing still more difficult.
The Conservatives have been accused of delaying the Wirral South poll, but Mawhinney said they would consider in the new year when voting should take place.

The Barnsley by-election represented a setback for the Socialist Labour Party set up by miners' union leader Arthur Scargill in protest at Labour's abandonment of traditional left-wing policy stances.
Its candidate, Ken Capstick won only 949 votes, just over five percent of the total.
"It is the final dismissal of the Socialist Labour Party. Being realistic, it is goodbye, isn't it," Dewar said.
